body_html:
Texting in Spanish has its own rhythm. People drop vowels, swap letters for sounds, laugh with long strings of jajaja and switch to voice messages without warning. If you only know textbook Spanish, a chat with friends or a partner can look like a code. This guide decodes the most common abbreviations, explains the tone behind them and gives you messages you can send today.

Key takeaways
  • Spanish laughs with jaja, not “haha”, because the Spanish j sounds like an English h.
  • q, xq, tb and tqm cover a huge share of everyday texts.
  • The opening ¿ and ¡ are often skipped in casual chats, but not in formal messages.
  • Voice notes are extremely common in many Spanish-speaking countries.
{{toc}}

How to laugh in Spanish

Because the Spanish j sounds like an English h, laughter is written jajaja. A short jaja is polite amusement; a long jajajajaja is real laughter. You’ll also see jeje (a cheeky or slightly awkward laugh) and jiji (giggly). Writing “haha” will be understood, but jaja instantly looks more natural.

{{image:2}}

Greetings and check-ins

  • ¿Qué tal? How’s it going? (everywhere)
  • ¿Qué onda? What’s up? (Mexico and Central America)
  • ¿Qué hubo? / ¿Quiubo? What’s up? (Colombia, Chile, Mexico)
  • ¿Todo bien? All good?
  • ¿Qué haces? What are you doing? (a very common opener)

Texting your partner in Spanish

Sweet messages don’t have to be long. These work in any country:

  • Buenos días, mi amor. ¿Dormiste bien? Good morning, my love. Did you sleep well?
  • Te extraño / Te echo de menos (Spain). I miss you.
  • Pensando en ti. Thinking of you.
  • Avísame cuando llegues. Let me know when you get there.
  • Que descanses. Sueña bonito. Rest well. Sweet dreams.

For affectionate nicknames to add to these, see {{link:spanish-terms-of-endearment|Spanish terms of endearment}}.

{{book:love-slowly}}

Punctuation, accents and tone

In casual chats many people skip the opening ¿ and ¡ and leave out accents. That is fine with friends. In work messages or with older relatives, full punctuation shows care, and accents can change meaning: si (if) vs sí (yes). Language organizations such as FundéuRAE regularly publish advice on writing correctly in digital messages.

Tone matters too. A one-word ok can feel cold; ¡Va, perfecto! (Mexico) or ¡Vale, perfecto! (Spain) feels friendlier. Diminutives soften everything: un ratito (a little while), ahorita (in a bit, in Mexico).

Voice notes and emojis

In many Spanish-speaking countries, voice notes (audios) are as common as text. Don’t be surprised by a two-minute audio in reply to a short question. It is great listening practice. Useful phrases: Te mando un audio (I’ll send you a voice note) and Ahora no puedo escuchar audios (I can’t listen to voice notes right now).

{{image:3}}

Making plans by text

Most texting is about logistics. These phrases will cover almost every plan:

  • ¿Nos vemos mañana? Shall we meet tomorrow? (in Spain, ¿Quedamos mañana?)
  • ¿A qué hora te viene bien? What time works for you?
  • Llego en cinco minutos. I’ll be there in five minutes.
  • Voy tarde, perdón. I’m running late, sorry.
  • Ya estoy aquí. I’m here now.
  • ¿Lo dejamos para otro día? Shall we leave it for another day?

A small warning about ahorita: in Mexico it can mean “right now”, “in a bit” or “who knows when”, depending on tone. If timing matters, ask for a time.

A sample chat

  • A: Holaa q tal tu día? (Hiii how was your day?)
  • B: Bien!! mucho trabajo jaja y tú? (Good!! lots of work haha and you?)
  • A: Tb, pero ya terminé. ¿Nos vemos para cenar? (Same, but I’m done now. Shall we meet for dinner?)
  • B: Siii, a las 8? Te mando la ubi (Yesss, at 8? I’ll send you the location)
  • A: Perfecto, nos vemos. Bss (Perfect, see you. Kisses)

Notice the doubled letters (Holaa, Siii) for enthusiasm, the missing opening question marks and ubi, short for ubicación (location). This is exactly how friends write in real life.

Texting at work

With colleagues or clients, keep it fuller: Hola, Laura. ¿Te viene bien que hablemos a las 10? Use complete words, accents and both question marks. Many people still end with a friendly Saludos (or Un saludo in Spain). For longer messages, see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.

Slang words like güey or parce are common in chats too; see {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}} for what they mean in each country.

Mistakes to avoid when texting in Spanish

  • Writing “haha”. Not wrong, but jaja looks native.
  • Using tqm with someone you just met. It means “love you lots”, too strong for a new acquaintance.
  • Translating “lol”. Some people use it, but jajaja is far more common.
  • Dropping accents in formal messages. It can look careless at work.

Texting is one of many everyday moments where small phrases make a big difference. See {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}} for more, or plan your next meeting with {{link:first-date-in-spanish|first date phrases in Spanish}}.

Final thoughts

Texting in Spanish is a wonderful way to practice: it is short, informal and full of real language. Start with a few abbreviations, laugh with jaja, and don’t be afraid to send a voice note back.

faq.q: How do you write “haha” in Spanish?
faq.a: Jaja or jajaja, because the Spanish j sounds like an English h. Jeje is a cheekier or slightly awkward laugh.

faq.q: What does tqm mean in Spanish?
faq.a: Tqm stands for te quiero mucho, “I love you lots”. It is used with partners, family and close friends.
Xq is short for porque (because) or por qué (why). The x stands for por, because the multiplication sign is read “por” in Spanish.
